questions.prompt: Under the shared responsibility model, what is always the customer's responsibility?

options.text: Their data, identity/access management, and configuration

questions.explanation: The provider secures the cloud itself, but the customer always secures what they put in it — data, IAM, and configuration.

questions.prompt: Which are common causes of cloud breaches? Select all that apply.

options.text: Secrets committed to code or images

questions.explanation: Public storage, over-permissive IAM, and committed secrets cause most cloud breaches; least-privilege scoped roles are the fix, not a cause.

questions.prompt: Containers share the host's ____, which makes their isolation weaker than a virtual machine's.
questions.explanation: Containers isolate via namespaces/cgroups but share the host kernel, so a kernel flaw can allow a container escape — unlike a VM with its own kernel.

questions.prompt: Match each cloud/container term to its meaning.

pairs.right: Who/what can do which actions on which resources
Breaking out of a container to the host or others
Checking an image for known-vulnerable packages

questions.explanation: IAM governs access, a container escape breaks isolation, image scanning finds vulnerable components, and a secrets manager keeps credentials out of code/images.

questions.prompt: Order a sound container image hardening pipeline.

items.text: Scan the image for known vulnerabilities
Run as a non-root user with dropped capabilities
Inject secrets at runtime (never bake them in)

questions.explanation: Start minimal, scan for vulnerabilities, run non-root with least capabilities, and inject secrets at runtime rather than embedding them in the image.

questions.prompt: Why shouldn't untrusted code run in a plain container as a security sandbox?

options.text: Containers share the host kernel, so a container escape can reach the host or other tenants
Containers are too slow for untrusted code
Containers cannot run code at all
Untrusted code always needs the internet

questions.explanation: Because containers share the kernel, they aren't a strong boundary for hostile code; use a VM or hardened sandbox for untrusted workloads.
